title: Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA)
summary: Describes the Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm, a modern way to create and verify digital signatures. It gives parameters for the edwards25519 and edwards448 curves, with an example implementation and test vectors.

eli5.summary: A digital signature is like a stamp only you can make that anyone can check. EdDSA is a modern, fast stamp that is hard to forge.

questions: what is the difference between ed25519 and ed448
how big is an ed25519 signature
subtitle: A modern digital signature scheme on Edwards curves, with small keys, deterministic signatures and two recommended variants.

tldr.problem: Digital signature schemes often need a fresh random number for every signature, are hard to implement without leaking secrets through timing, and need costly checks on untrusted public values.
tldr.mechanism: EdDSA is a variant of Schnorr signatures on Edwards curves. The RFC fixes its parameters for two curves, edwards25519 and edwards448, and gives an implementation-oriented description, sample code and test vectors.
tldr.outcome: It yields Ed25519 (32-byte public keys, 64-byte signatures) and Ed448 (57-byte public keys, 114-byte signatures). The RFC is Informational and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Security level
facts.value: Ed25519 about 128 bits, Ed448 about 224 bits

today: RFC 8032 is an Informational RFC from the IRTF. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What EdDSA Is and Why
sections.content:
The Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA) is a variant of Schnorr's signature system that uses (possibly twisted) Edwards curves. The RFC describes it in an implementation-oriented way and provides sample code and test vectors to help adoption.

It lists six advantages: high performance on a variety of platforms; no need for a unique random number per signature; more resilience to side-channel attacks; small public keys (32 or 57 bytes) and signatures (64 or 114 bytes) for Ed25519 and Ed448; "complete" formulas that avoid expensive point validation of untrusted public values; and collision resilience, which holds only for PureEdDSA.

Ed25519 aims at around the 128-bit security level and Ed448 at around the 224-bit level. The RFC notes that a sufficiently large quantum computer would be able to break both.
sections.eli5: A signature proves a message really came from you. EdDSA is a recipe for making short, hard-to-fake signatures quickly, without needing a lucky random number each time.

sections.title: The Generic EdDSA Design
sections.content:
Generic EdDSA has 11 parameters, including a prime p, a bit length b, a hash function H, a cofactor exponent c, curve constants d and a, a base point B, a prime order L and a prehash function PH. The RFC says this generic system is not meant to be implemented directly. You implement a particular parameter choice such as Ed25519 or Ed448.

A private key is a b-bit string. It is hashed, and part of the hash is turned into a secret scalar s. The public key is the encoding of the point [s]B. The rest of the hash output is kept for use when signing.

Points on the curve form a group under addition. The addition formulas are complete: they are valid for all points on the curve with no exceptions, and the neutral element is (0,1).
sections.eli5: Think of a secret number that you use to make a public number. Anyone can see the public one, but nobody can work backwards to your secret.

sections.title: Signing and Verifying
sections.content:
A signature is the string ENC(R) || ENC(S), which is 2*b bits long. The signer computes a value r by hashing the second half of the hashed private key together with the message. From it comes the point R = [r]B and S = (r + H(ENC(R) || ENC(A) || PH(M)) * s) mod L. Because r is derived from the key and the message, signatures are deterministic.

To verify, the receiver parses A and R as curve points and S as an integer in the range 0 to L-1. It computes h = H(ENC(R) || ENC(A) || M) and checks the group equation [2^c * S] B = 2^c * R + [2^c * h] A. The signature is rejected if parsing fails, including S being out of range, or if the equation does not hold.
sections.eli5: Signing mixes your secret with the message to make a stamp. Checking uses the public number to see that the stamp fits that exact message.

sections.title: The Five Instances
sections.content:
The RFC instantiates EdDSA for the edwards25519 and edwards448 curves, in PureEdDSA and HashEdDSA forms, plus a contextualized extension of Ed25519. That gives five parameter sets: Ed25519, Ed25519ctx, Ed25519ph, Ed448 and Ed448ph.

PureEdDSA signs the message itself. HashEdDSA first hashes the message with a prehash function. PureEdDSA keeps collision resilience but needs two passes over the input. HashEdDSA allows a single-pass interface, which suits APIs that assume signatures need only one pass.

Ed25519 uses p = 2^255 - 19, b = 256 and SHA-512. Ed448 uses p = 2^448 - 2^224 - 1, b = 456 and SHAKE256 with 114 octets of output. Ed25519ctx and Ed448 accept a context of at most 255 octets that must match byte for byte for verification to succeed. Plain Ed25519 must have an empty context.
sections.eli5: There are five versions of the stamp, like small, medium and large rubber stamps. Some read the whole message in one go, some shrink it first.

sections.title: Keys, Encodings and Sizes
sections.content:
Everything is coded as octet strings, with integers in little-endian order. For Ed25519 a point is encoded as the 32-octet little-endian y-coordinate, with the least significant bit of the x-coordinate copied into the top bit of the final octet. Ed448 does the same with 57 octets.

An Ed25519 private key is 32 octets of cryptographically secure random data. The public key is generated by hashing the private key with SHA-512, pruning the lower half of the digest (clearing the lowest three bits of the first octet, clearing the highest bit of the last octet and setting the second highest), and multiplying the base point by the resulting scalar. A signature is 32 octets of R followed by 32 octets of S.

Decoding checks that the y-coordinate is below p and that a square root for x exists, and decoding fails otherwise. The RFC also gives Python sample code and test vectors for each variant.
sections.eli5: Keys and signatures are just fixed-length strings of bytes, like a license plate that always has the same number of characters.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC covers several practical points. Because the signing step derives its random value from the key and message, signatures are deterministic, which protects against attacks arising from signing with bad randomness. Private key generation still needs randomness.

Implementations can resist side-channel attacks by executing the same instructions and memory accesses for any private key; complete addition formulas make that easier. The RFC states that its own example implementations do not attempt to be side-channel silent.

  • Signatures are not malleable, thanks to the check that decoded S is smaller than the group order.
  • Contexts SHOULD be a constant string chosen by the protocol and SHOULD NOT be used opportunistically.
  • Ed25519ph and Ed448ph SHOULD NOT be used, because prehashing makes them more vulnerable to hash weaknesses.
  • If 128-bit strength is enough, Ed25519 is RECOMMENDED; otherwise Ed448 is RECOMMENDED.

Receivers should avoid signing large amounts of data at once, since the whole message has to be buffered before the signature can be verified.
sections.eli5: Because the stamp is made from your secret and the message, it never depends on luck. Just keep your secret hidden, and do not let the stamp machine give away clues while it works.
